reason: Start with the turning sensors: their placement in fluid-filled canals seems relevant to detecting head movement.
expectation: I expect to assemble a sensor for head rotation, though the exact mechanism may need explaining.

alternatives.reason: Tilt and acceleration sensors also fit the balance goal, but I chose to start with turning.

effect: The canal sensors respond to fluid movement when a turn starts or changes; next I can build the other balance sensors.
reaction: The connection between fluid movement and bending sensors is clear.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should address tilt and acceleration.
expectation: I expect the weighted membranes to couple to the hair cells so they can sense tilt or acceleration, though I am unsure exactly how.

effect: The weighted membranes shift over hair cells during tilt or straight-line acceleration, completing the second sensor type.
reaction: The paired tilt and forward-motion examples clarify what these organs detect.
reason: This is the only offered combination; it should bring the two balance-sensing systems together.
expectation: I expect a combined set of balance organs that detects changes in rotation and straight-line motion as well as gravity.

effect: The rotation and gravity-sensing organs are now grouped beside the cochlea; they still need a connection to the brain.
reaction: The placement links balance to the earlier hearing construction, though this step adds little about function.
reason: The only offered combination should connect the balance organs to the brainstem.
expectation: I expect nerve pathways to carry information from the balance sensors toward the brainstem.

effect: The balance organs now have nerve pathways toward the brainstem; reflex and body connections remain.
reaction: The nerve route is clear, though this result adds little about how the signals are used.
reason: Connect the reflex pathways first to link the sensors to eye and posture control.
expectation: I expect pathways from the balance nerves through the brainstem toward eye-movement and postural circuits.

alternatives.reason: Adding the organs to the body would also advance the goal, but I want to connect the reflexes first.

effect: The balance pathways now branch from the brainstem toward eye-movement and postural circuits; they still need to be connected to the body.
reaction: The branching makes the two reflex destinations clear, though it does not yet show either reflex in action.
reason: This is the only offered combination and should connect the completed pathways to the body.
expectation: I expect the balance organs and reflex pathways to join the existing brain, eyes and posture controls, possibly showing their response to head movement.

effect: The completed body shows how balance signals help steady the eyes during a head turn and contribute to posture alongside other sensory information.
reaction: The opposing eye movement makes the opening scenario concrete; the posture inset is less detailed.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the reflex pathways to the body was most worthwhile: the planned paired views show why the sensors matter when turning toward a friend.

leastWorthwhile.text: Grouping the two sensor types beside the cochlea added little functional explanation after their separate constructions.

surprise.text: The weighted membrane shifts over hair cells both when the head tilts and when it moves forward, linking gravity and straight-line acceleration to the same organs.

arbitrary.text: No action felt purposeless, although grouping the balance organs was a predictable assembly step rather than a meaningful discovery. The offered compatible options guided the choices.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: the final head-turn example connects the constructed pathways to an everyday action, although several intermediate fittings felt procedural.
